newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat ends up on harsh wheat belt weather.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat ends up on harsh wheat belt weather.

text.p: Harsh spring weather in several key wheat growing regions of the U.S. boosted CBOT soft red winter wheat futures to a strongly higher close, traders said.
The concerns for wheat stretched from the spring wheat belt to the hard red winter growing states of the U.S. Plains.
"They're worried about cold weather forecasts in northern Texas and in Oklahoma," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
Meteorologists early Thursday said frigid cold could damage winter wheat this weekend from Kansas to Texas.
Lows could dip to 18 degrees Fahrenheit in southwest Kansas and 25 degrees in the Texas Panhandle, they said.
"We are talking about the liklihood of some damaging cold temperatures for the southern Plains wheat this weekend," said Joel Burgio, meteorologist for Weather Services Corp.
Wheat closed 7-1/2 to nine cents per bushel higher, with May up 7-1/2 at $3.93 a bushel.
The market again took note of cold, wet weather in the upper Midwest spring wheat growing areas which could delay seeding of that crop.
College students joined sandbagging efforts Thursday ahead of the expected record crest of the Red River.
The Red River Valley of the U.S. is the key spring wheat growing region.

"The wheat market is responding to weather in a big way," said John Kleist, director of agricultural research for ING Futures and Options. "Supposedly that cold front earlier in the week didn't do much damage but now some people are saying it did do some damage. And the cold front moving in this week is supposed to be even colder. There could be some decent damage to this wheat crop. It looks like it's a potential problem."
While there was concern about the spring wheat growing areas, most of the attention focused on the key hard red winter growing region of the U.S. Great Plains.
The weather-talk grabbed the attention of the futures pit and also stirred concern in the cash markets.
Forecasts for crop-threatening cold over the next few days was the main focus of the hard red winter wheat market, with movement slow and basis bids steady, cash dealers said.

"We dodged a bullet the other night and are hoping to be able to dodge another one but it doesn't look very good," one Oklahoma grain dealer said, noting forecasts for a sharp drop in temperatures Friday and Saturday nights.
Dealers in Oklahoma and Kansas said crops probably survived the early-week cold mostly unscathed.
But the greatest threat was still ahead, some sources said.
"There may be a little bit of damage this weekend," one Kansas dealer said.
USDA's weekly export sales report Thursday was bullish for corn and soybeans and neutral for wheat, traders said.
USDA said U.S. net export sales of wheat during the week ended April 3 totaled 216,900 tonnes, near the low end of expectations for 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes.

In spread trading, Term Commodities did one million bushels of May/July at 3-1/4 to 3-1/2 cents, premium July and Cargill Investor Services did 700,000 July/May at three cents, premium July, traders said.
In outright trading, FIMAT Futures, A.B. N-Amro bought one million July while Rand Financial and Refco Inc each bought 1.5 million bushels of July, traders said.
Cargill Inc sold 1.5 million bushels of July, the traders said.
Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 20,000 contracts, below the 20,771 traded Wednesday.
In wheat options, ADM Investor Services sold 500 July $3.40 puts at 17-3/4 cents, FIMAT Futures bought 400 July $3.70 puts at 10 cents and sold 400 July $3.80 puts at 13-1/2 cents, traders said.
Wheat options volume was estimated at 15,000 contracts, above the 10,157 traded Wednesday.
